title: A hymn in Maru
hook: Maru holds the long Solhe and Kabir's song of the true warrior

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Maru, and your line was courage. Did you do the small, slightly scary thing, and did you do it without frightening anyone? Day one thousand one hundred seven.

A drum sounds in the sky. A target is struck. A fighter has stepped onto the field, and the poem says: now is the time to fight. That's how a verse begins near the end of Raga Maru, and the voice is not a general's. It's Kabir, the weaver-poet whose verses the Gurus gathered into the Granth. Maru also holds the long Solhe, great extended hymns of the Gurus. But today we go to Kabir's battlefield, and find out what kind of warrior he means.
screen: `A DRUM IN THE SKY.` → `A WEAVER ON THE BATTLEFIELD.` → `KABIR'S WARRIOR.`

segments.voice: Here's Kabir's hymn, given in plain English, not word for word. The battle drum sounds in the sky; the target is struck. The warrior has entered the field; now is the time to fight. Then the lines at its heart: the true warrior is the one who fights for the sake of the deen, and who, even cut apart piece by piece, never leaves the field. Two things are worth hearing closely. The first is the drum in the sky. Some readers hear that sky as the inner sky of the mind, where the battle Kabir means is fought: against ego, greed, fear and the rest. The poem sounds like a battlefield and points inward. The second is the word deen. Some translators give it as the poor and helpless, so the true warrior fights for the defenseless. Others give it as faith, or the path of righteousness. Both readings have their commentators, and the hymn bears them both. Either way, the warrior isn't fighting for glory, plunder or a grudge. He fights for something beyond himself. And notice what makes him a warrior: not winning. Staying. Cut apart, he doesn't leave the field. Some Sikhs connect this verse to the ideal of the saint-soldier, a person of prayer who is also ready to stand up for others. Yesterday we heard nirbhau and nirvair, without fear and without hate. Kabir gives that courage a body and a place to stand: in the field, for the deen, all the way through. That's today's line: the true warrior.
screen: `THE DRUM SOUNDS; THE FIELD IS SET.` · `THE BATTLE IN THE MIND'S SKY.` · `FIGHTING FOR THE HELPLESS.` · `NOT WINNING: STAYING.` · then, large: `THE TRUE WARRIOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay on the field. Sit, feet down, back steady. Notice the first thing that pulls you away: an itch, a thought, a plan for later. Don't fight it angrily. Just stay. Each time the mind leaves, notice where it went, and come back to the breath, as calmly as a soldier returning to post. That's the whole sit: leaving, and returning, without a grudge. If you pray, you can say Waheguru each time you return. If you don't, simply say back, silently. Later today, listen to one Maru shabad, Kabir's if you can find it. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Maru. Kabir's song of the true warrior, who fights for the deen, the helpless or the right, and never leaves the field. Today's word.
Your line: the true warrior. Once today, stand up for someone with less power than you, even in a small way, and stay with it a little longer than is comfortable. Day one thousand one hundred seven.

howItsDone: Kabir's hymn of the true warrior is sung in kirtan in Raga Maru, and its closing lines are quoted by some Sikhs when speaking of the saint-soldier ideal of the Khalsa.
